River restoration project reshapes downtown waterfront

The city's decade-long effort to restore the river channel through downtown reached a milestone this week, as engineers removed the last section of concrete culvert that had confined the water since the 1950s.

Officials say the project, which cost roughly forty million dollars, is intended to reduce flooding, improve water quality, and reconnect the waterfront with the surrounding neighborhoods, which have been separated from the water for two generations.

"This is the biggest change to this stretch of the river in living memory," said the project's lead engineer at a ceremony held on the newly opened riverbank path. "We expect to see fish returning to spawn here within a few years, and residents are already using the new trail every day."

The restored channel meanders through a series of new wetlands designed to filter runoff before it reaches the river, a feature that planners say sets the project apart from earlier, purely cosmetic waterfront redevelopments in other cities.

Construction on the final phase, a pedestrian bridge connecting the two riverbanks, is expected to finish next spring, weather permitting, according to the city's public works department.
